נַחַל סַעַר (וָאדִי חַשַׁבֶּה) הוא נחל ה:
Nahal Sa'ar (Wadi Hashabeh) is a stream that flows between the northern Golan Heights and the Hermon ridge. The stream is known chiefly for the Sa'ar Waterfall, located near Route 99, and is characterized by an impressive flow after the rains.
The stream empties into Nahal Hermon about 500 meters southwest of the Banias spring.
גבעת האֵם (נקראת בערבית תל אבו חנזיר) הי: Giv'at HaEm (known in Arabic as Tel Abu Hanzir) is a basalt hill 196 meters above sea level located on the slopes of the Golan, at the edge of the Hula Valley. Like Kfar Szold, which lies about a kilometer and a half to the south, the hill is also named after Henrietta Szold, who was called the "Mother of Youth Aliyah".
עֵינַת הוא קיבוץ באזור השרון השייך למועצ: Einat is a kibbutz in the Sharon region belonging to the Drom HaSharon Regional Council. It lies southwest of Rosh HaAyin, and the only access road to it branches off Route 444, which connects Rosh HaAyin with Petah Tikva. In addition, the route of Highway 6 passes a few dozen meters west of the kibbutz, but does not lead to it.
נמל תל אביב הוא נמל על חוף הים התיכון שפ: The Tel Aviv Port is a port on the Mediterranean coast that operated at the mouth of the Yarkon River in northwestern Tel Aviv-Yafo in the years 1938–1965 and was called "the first Hebrew port". The establishment of the port was considered a significant step in the development of Hebrew shipping during the Mandate period. Since the first decade of the 21st century, the port compound has served as a leisure and entertainment complex.
נחל גוברין הוא נחל אכזב בשפלת יהודה, שרא:
Nahal Guvrin is an ephemeral stream in the Judean Lowlands (Shephelah), which begins in the Hebron Hills and ends at Nahal Lachish. The stream flows in a general northwesterly direction.
The stream drains an area of about 204 km², from the Hebron Hills (the area of the villages of Dura and Tapuah) at an elevation of about 850 meters above sea level, down to its confluence with Nahal Lachish after about 48 km.
מצפה מודיעין הוא מגדל תצפית שריפות ביער: Mitzpe Modi'in is a fire lookout tower in the Ben Shemen Forest, one of 42 fire lookout towers erected in the forests of the Jewish National Fund (KKL). They were intended to serve as observation posts for warning of and protection against fires. Since the late 1990s, in light of technological developments in detecting fire outbreaks, the towers are mostly unmanned.
מִדּרֶשֶׁת בֶּן-גּוּרִיּוֹן היא יישוב קה: Midreshet Ben-Gurion is a community settlement in Sde Zin in the Ramat HaNegev region, near Kibbutz Sde Boker, between Beersheba and Mitzpe Ramon. It includes a number of educational and research institutions. Most of the settlement's activity is operated by the Midreshet Sde Boker corporation; alongside Midreshet Ben-Gurion lies the "Ben-Gurion's Tomb National Park".
יער מיתר הוא יער נטוע בדרום ישראל, המקיף: Meitar Forest is a planted forest in southern Israel surrounding the town of Meitar to the north and east. The forest covers an area of about 8,200 dunams and lies at an elevation of about 450 m above sea level. It is a central component of the region's ecological and scenic landscape, contributing to the quality of life of the area's residents and serving as a recreation and leisure site.
כְּפַר גִּלְעָדִי הוא קיבוץ באצבע הגליל: Kfar Giladi is a kibbutz in the Galilee Panhandle near Metula and Kiryat Shmona, belonging to the Upper Galilee Regional Council. The kibbutz was formed as a result of a merger carried out in the 1920s and 1930s between Kfar Giladi, Tel Hai and Kibbutz Tiberias. South of the kibbutz (within the bounds of the former Tel Hai) now stands the Kiryat Shmona University in the Galilee.
זִכְרוֹן יַעֲקֹב היא מועצה מקומית במחוז:
Zichron Ya'akov is a local council in the Haifa District of Israel. It was founded as a moshava on 6 December 1882 by Hovevei Zion immigrants from Romania, and was the second moshava of the First Aliyah (after Rishon LeZion).
The moshava sits on Hotem HaCarmel, the southern part of the Carmel ridge. It was declared a local council in 1950.
גן לאומי ירקון הוא גן לאומי המשלב כיום ש: Yarkon National Park is a national park that today combines two sites: one is Tel Afek, entered from Route 483, between Petah Tikva and Rosh HaAyin, and the other is the sources of the Yarkon River, accessed from Route 5 or Route 40, via the entrance to the Baptist Village. The park has sites to visit alongside expanses of lawn, trees and water, for recreation and leisure.
יער יתיר הוא יער נטוע הנמצא בחבל יתיר, כ: Yatir Forest is a planted forest located in the Yatir region, about 30 km northeast of Beersheba. Its planted area extends over 37,000 dunams. It is the largest planted forest in Israel, and according to KKL-JNF the largest man-made forest in the world planted in a semi-arid region. It is bordered on the east by the communities of Har Amasa and Beit Yatir, and on the north by Livne (Shani) and Asa'el.
מִכְמוֹרֶת הוא מושב בעמק חפר, כ-2 ק\"מ מ:
Michmoret is a moshav in the Hefer Valley, about 2 km south of Hadera and about 6 km north of Netanya. It is part of the Emek Hefer Regional Council, and is the northernmost settlement in it.
The moshav is adjacent to the mouth of Nahal Alexander on the Mediterranean coast. Next to the moshav is a bay that once served as an ancient harbor, and the Ramot Yam secondary school within the Mevo'ot Yam youth village.
פארק עֲדֻלָּם, או בשמו המלא פארק מערות ע:
Adullam Park, or by its full name Adullam Caves Park, is a park in the eastern Judean Lowlands in the Adullam region, containing archaeological remains from various periods. The park is named after the biblical city of Adullam, mentioned in the Bible, which is identified with a tel located within the park.
Development of the park began after the completion of the separation barrier east of the park, toward the Hebron Hills.
שער הַגַּיְא (בערבית: باب الواد – בָּאב: Sha'ar HaGai (Arabic: باب الواد – Bab al-Wad) is a narrow entrance passage from the lowlands into the Jerusalem Hills, located today on Highway 1, at the 35th kilometer from Tel Aviv. Nearby is the Sha'ar HaGai Interchange. From Sha'ar HaGai, Highway 1 continues eastward toward Jerusalem for about six kilometers through a narrow valley along the bed of Nahal Nahshon (Wadi Ali) as far as the Sho'eva area.
נַחַל פְּרָצִים הוא נחל אכזב בדרום מדבר: Nahal Peratzim is an ephemeral stream in the southern Judean Desert. Nahal Peratzim originates in the Amiaz Plain, which it drains; it flows northeast, is 5.5 km long, and at its end joins the drainage basin of Nahal Heimar and Nahal Zohar, emptying into the Zohar Valley and the Dead Sea north of Mount Sodom. The stream's gorge reaches a depth of about 50 meters and is only a few meters wide.
גני רמת הנדיב הוא פארק טבע רחב-ידיים, שה: Ramat HaNadiv Gardens is an expansive nature park established around the burial plot of Baron Benjamin Edmond de Rothschild, south of Zichron Ya'akov. The site is dedicated to Baron Rothschild in recognition of his great contribution to the Jewish people. Rothschild died in 1934. In the early 1950s his remains were brought for burial at Ramat HaNadiv, and the park (which had existed before then) was dedicated to his memory.
נְאוֹת סְמָדַר הוא קיבוץ בדרום הערבה סמו: Neot Semadar is a kibbutz in the southern Arava near the Shizafon Junction, on Route 40, belonging to the Hevel Eilot Regional Council. The kibbutz is a member of the TAKAM (United Kibbutz Movement). The kibbutz was founded as the "Shizafon" Nahal outpost in 1980, and after it failed to get off the ground, the Neot Semadar group settled there in 1989 and established a community centered on ecological and organic themes. The settlement extends over an area of about 800 dunams.
נַחַל אֲלֶכְּסַנְדֶּר (בעבר: נהר אסְכַּנ: Nahal Alexander (formerly: the Iskanderuna River) is a stream that flows from the Samarian Hills to the Mediterranean Sea. For most of its course it flows through the Hefer Valley. The stream's mouth lies north of Netanya, between the moshavim of Michmoret and Beit Yanai. The stream drains the Nablus area and central Samaria, as well as part of the Sharon. The stream is about 32 km long. The lower part of the stream and its surroundings are a declared national park.
עין סהרונים הוא מעיין קטן, היחיד במכתש ר:
Ein Saharonim is a small spring, the only one in Makhtesh Ramon, and the largest and most important source of water in the makhtesh. The spring is located in the Mezuke Zinim (Zin Cliffs) Nature Reserve, near Metzad Saharonim – an ancient way station.
The name Ein Saharonim derives from the drooping saharon (acacia mistletoe) plant that grows in the area. In Arabic the spring is called al-Mahla ("the dry spring", "the spring of drought"), like the Nabataean khan Qasr al-Mahla.
נחל חווארים הוא נחל אכזב בנגב המרכזי, דר:
Nahal Havarim is an ephemeral stream in the central Negev, south of Midreshet Ben-Gurion and north of the town of Mitzpe Ramon. It begins at Route 40 near Tziporim Junction and ends at the foot of Ma'ale HaGar, where it joins Nahal Avdat and together with it forms Nahal Zin. Nahal Karkash connects to Nahal Havarim roughly at its midpoint.
Nahal Havarim enters the Zin Valley, which lies between the Avdat Plateau and Ramat HaNegev.
עין עקב הוא שמם של שני מעיינות הבוקעים ע: Ein Akev is the name of two springs that emerge along the channel of Nahal Akev on the Avdat Plateau in the central Negev, southeast of the community settlement of Midreshet Ben-Gurion and near Nahal Zin and Ein Avdat. The name derives from the Arabic name of the place, Ein Umm Ka'b, meaning "spring of the heel". The stone after which the spring is named is a black flint rock found at Upper Ein Akev, which stands out sharply from its white surroundings.
מִצְפֵּה רָמוֹן היא מועצה מקומית במחוז ה:
Mitzpe Ramon is a local council in the Southern District of Israel.
Mitzpe Ramon lies in the center of the Negev Highlands, on the northern rim of Makhtesh Ramon, about 80 km south of Beersheba and about 150 km north of Eilat. Its jurisdiction covers 64,500 dunams and it has about 5,047 residents. It was founded in 1953 as a work camp for the laborers who paved the road to Eilat, and became a permanent settlement in 1956.
מוֹאָב הוא שמו של חבל ארץ בעבר הירדן המז:
Moab is the name of a region in eastern Transjordan during the Israelite period, corresponding largely to the Iron Age, from the end of the 2nd millennium BCE to the 6th century BCE. According to the sources, Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, between the Dead Sea escarpment and the Arabian Desert, within the territory of the present-day Kingdom of Jordan.
Moab is a predominantly mountainous land, and the mountains between Nahal Zered and Nahal Arnon are called the Mountains of Moab.
בקעת תִּמְנָע היא בקעה בשוליים המערביים: The Timna Valley is a valley on the western margins of the southern Arava, about 25 kilometers north of Eilat. The horseshoe-shaped valley extends over an area of about 60 square kilometers and is bounded by steep cliffs on three sides. It is drained by Nahal Timna in the north and Nahal Nehushtan in the south, which flow to the Arava east of it. At its center rises Mount Timna to a height of 453 meters. The area has an extreme desert climate.
שמורת נחל הבניאס או שמורת נחל חרמון היא: The Nahal Banias Nature Reserve, or Nahal Hermon Nature Reserve, is a nature reserve located at the foot of Mount Hermon, at the meeting point between the Golan Heights and the Hula Valley, near the community of Snir. It extends along Nahal Hermon from the area of the Banias springs down to the head of the sources of the Jordan. The reserve was declared in 1977 over an area of about 800 dunams. In 2009 the reserve was expanded and a further 500 dunams or so were added upstream, and since then the reserve's area has stood at about 1,300 dunams.
קרני חיטין הוא שמו של הר געש כבוי בגליל:
The Horns of Hattin (Karnei Hittin) is the name of an extinct volcano in the Lower Galilee, near Mount Arbel; its maximum height is 326 meters, and it lies about 5 km west of Tiberias, above the city. The mountain owes its name to its two peaks, which are shaped like horns. It is thought that its two peaks – known as the "horns" – are volcanic plugs exposed by erosion. In 2007 the area around the mountain was declared a national park.
From the Horns of Hattin one can see the Sea of Galilee (Kinneret), Gilead, the Golan and the Galilee.
עֵין בּוֹקֵק הוא מתחם התיירות והבילוי הע: Ein Bokek is the main tourism and leisure complex on the Israeli side of the Dead Sea. The complex lies within the Tamar Regional Council, on the shores of Pond 5 in the southern basin of the lake, at 392 meters below sea level. The Ein Bokek hotels were built on the alluvial fan of Nahal Zohar, between the lakeshore to the east and Route 90 to the west, and the site is about a kilometer and a half long from north to south. The place is named after the Ein Bokek springs in Nahal Bokek.
המכתש הקטן (בשמו המדויק: מכתש חֲצֵרָה) ה:
The Small Crater (HaMakhtesh HaKatan; by its precise name, Makhtesh Hatzera) is an erosional crater, the third largest of the five makhteshim of the Negev and the Sinai Peninsula.
The Small Crater is located in the Hatzera ridge and is therefore also called Makhtesh Hatzera (Arabic: الخضيرة – al-Khudayra – "the threshing floor of the palms"). It is the easternmost makhtesh in the series of craters formed in the anticlines of the Negev Highlands and northern Sinai, which include Makhtesh Ramon, the Large Crater (HaMakhtesh HaGadol) and the Arif makhteshim.
In June 2019 the state declared the crater a nature reserve.
הר עמשא הוא הר בהרי חברון, מדרום ליישוב:
Har Amasa (Mount Amasa) is a mountain in the Hebron Hills, south of the community of Har Amasa and 13 km north of Arad. The mountain is 859 meters above sea level, and from its summit one can look out over the southern Judean Desert and the Arad Valley, the northern Negev Highlands and, to the north, the Hebron Hills. 
The mountain lies within the jurisdiction of the Tamar Regional Council, and around it is a declared nature reserve, the "Har Amasa Nature Reserve". The mountain received its name in modern times after Amasa son of Jether, who was commander of Absalom's army and later commander of King David's army.
מקום קברו של רבי שמעון בר יוחאי (רשב\"י): The burial place of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (Rashbi), a Tanna of the 2nd century, lies according to the Midrash in ancient Meron. Today, the tomb on Mount Meron is regarded as a matter of Jewish consensus and is among the most famous in the Land of Israel and the world, and the second most visited religious site in the country by annual number of visitors, after the Western Wall. The hillula held at the site every year on Lag BaOmer is the largest annual civil-religious event in Israel. A common custom is to perform the chalakah there, the ceremony of a boy's first haircut at the age of three.
שבלול החרמון (שם מדעי: Helix pachya, בעב: The Hermon snail (scientific name: Helix pachya, formerly Helix texta) is a snail of the family Helicidae and the order of air-breathing land snails (pulmonates) that lives on land. The Hermon snail is a species endemic to the Land of Israel and is found only on the slopes of Mount Hermon, mainly in the Nahal Hermon Nature Reserve. In the past the Hermon snail was classified under the species Helix texta, but after re-examination it became clear that it is the same species as Helix pachya, and it was therefore reclassified under that name, since the species Helix pachya had been described first.
Hod Akev is a residual hill (inselberg) located at the Zin Cliffs (Mezuke Zinim). The mountain is conical in shape, and its height is about 576 meters above sea level. The mountain is part of the Avdat Plateau.

The mountain takes its name from the nearby Nahal Akev and Ein Akev; the name derives from the Arabic word ka'b (كَعْب).
From the summit there is a wide view over Nahal Akev, Ramat Boker and the Zin Valley. The ascent of the mountain on its northern side along the Israel National Trail is extremely steep, and includes climbing with the aid of iron rungs.
In the past several hikers were killed climbing the cliff.
מקדש הנמרים הוא אתר ארכאולוגי, בו התגלה: The Leopards Temple is an archaeological site where an open-air temple that served as a prehistoric cult site was discovered. The site lies east of the access road to the community of Shaharut, northeast of Ovda Airport in the Ovda Valley. The place is one of some 160 open-air temples discovered so far in the Negev and eastern Sinai, and it was in use for about 4,000 years, from the middle of the 6th millennium BCE (the Late Neolithic period) until the first half of the 2nd millennium BCE (the Middle Bronze Age).
עמודי שלמה הם צורות סלע, הנראות למתבונן:
Solomon's Pillars are rock formations that appear to the viewer as giant stone columns. The pillars are located in the Timna Valley, north of Eilat. The pillars were formed by weathering caused by wind and water along fault lines in the red sandstone. Solomon's Pillars rise to a height of about 40 meters.
The impressive shape of the pillars, which look like the columns of a temple, led the ancient Egyptians who mined copper in the valley to build at their foot a temple to Hathor, the goddess of the mines, a temple that was later also used by the Midianites.
נַחַל צֶאֱלִים (בערבית: وادِي السيّال- ו: Nahal Tze'elim (Arabic: وادِي السيّال – Wadi as-Sayyal) is one of the largest ephemeral streams among the Judean Desert streams descending to the Dead Sea; its length from its source to its mouth is about 32 km. The stream's drainage basin covers about 287 km². The stream drains the southeastern Hebron Hills near the community of Ma'on, continues north of Arad and empties into the Dead Sea north of Masada. In addition to many water pools (gevim), which fill each year after the winter rain floods, four springs emerge in the stream.
נַחַל גִּשְׁרוֹן (בערבית: وادِي جسرية –:
Nahal Gishron (Arabic: وادِي جسرية – Wadi Jasriya) is an ephemeral stream in the Eilat Mountains. 
Its upper tributaries begin in the area of Ras an-Naqab near the Netafim Crossing. The stream descends steeply to its mouth at the Red Sea in Taba, Egypt. 
The stream has hiking trails along its upper sections, from which there are views of its landscapes. The stream has several cliffs where rappelling can be done.
The final section of the Israel National Trail begins in the stream, ending at the Eilat Field School at the foot of Mount Tzfahot.
לטרון הוא רכס בעמק איילון, במרחק של כ-15:
Latrun is a ridge in the Ayalon Valley, about 15 kilometers west of the city of Jerusalem. The ridge commands the road to Jerusalem, is considered an important strategic objective, and major battles were fought there, from biblical times to the Six-Day War.
The name originates in a corruption of the name of the Latrun fortress, a Crusader castle built on the site that was called in French "Le toron des chevaliers" ("the tower of the knights" in free translation). According to another hypothesis, the name derives from the Latin Castellum bonu Latronis, the castle of the good thief.
אמות המים של קיסריה היא מערכת של אמות מי: The aqueducts of Caesarea are a system of aqueducts that carried water to the city of Caesarea in antiquity. The aqueducts of Caesarea functioned throughout the city's existence – from its founding in the days of Herod until the 13th century, when it was destroyed in the days of the Mamluk sultan Baybars. Although Caesarea was built over a high water table, which allowed water supply by means of wells, the city's builders provided a supply of running water to the city, as was customary in the great cities of the Roman period. The system was composed of several different parts.
כביש הנפט (באנגלית: Petroleum Road, מכונ: The Petroleum Road (Kvish HaNeft; also known as the Oil Route) is a rutted, privately owned longitudinal asphalt road in the Golan Heights, 47 km long, extending from the Syrian border near Mount Peres in the eastern central Golan to the Lebanese border, near the village of Ghajar. The road takes its name from the "Trans-Arabian Pipeline" (Trans-Arabian Pipeline Company, the Tapline), along which it was built. This road is a small part of a continuous route that accompanies the oil pipeline along its entire length.
חוּרבַת חָנוֹת (בערבית: ח'רבת אל-ח'אן) ה: Horvat Hanot (Arabic: Khirbet al-Khan) is a ruin on the slopes of the Jerusalem Hills toward the transition to the Judean Lowlands, about a kilometer west of Moshav Mata. The ruin was a wayfarers' inn (khan) from the Mamluk period; the inn served travelers on the Caesar's Road (Derech HaKeisar), which was part of the Roman road from Jerusalem and Bethlehem to the lowlands and Beit Guvrin, and it ceased to function during the Ottoman period in the Land of Israel. At the site are a colorful mosaic floor of a Byzantine-period church, a winepress and a storage pool.
מבצר נמרוד (ידוע גם בשמות קַלְעַת נַמרוּ: Nimrod Fortress (also known as Qal'at Namrud and Qal'at as-Subeiba – Arabic: قلعة الصبيبة) is an archaeological site from the Hellenistic period and the Middle Ages, containing the remains of a large fortress built over the years by Ayyubid and Mamluk armies. The fortress sits at the top of a narrow ridge at an elevation of about 800 meters above sea level, at the foot of Mount Hermon, about 3 kilometers southwest of the community of Neve Ativ and about 1,300 meters northeast of a tributary of Nahal Sa'ar. The site is a declared national park.
מצודת כ\"ח (שמה נֶהֱגֶה \"מצודת כוח\"; נ:
Metzudat Koach (its name, written with the Hebrew letters for 28, is pronounced "Metzudat Koach"; it is also called "Metzudat Yesha" and "Nabi Yusha", after the ruins of the nearby Arab village of Nabi Yusha) is a Tegart fort in the Northern District, about 10 km south of Kiryat Shmona. The fort is named after the 28 fighters killed in its capture during the War of Independence.
The fort today serves as a Border Police base, and beside it stand a memorial and a mass grave in which 19 of those who fell in the battles at the site are buried. In early 2014 the Re'ut (Comradeship) Museum, commemorating the battles and those who fell there, was opened next to the fort.
מְצַד זוֹהַר הוא שמם של שני מבנים עתיקים: Metzad Zohar is the name of two ancient structures in Nahal Zohar, west of Route 90. The eastern structure is the "Israelite" Metzad Zohar, located near the stream's outlet to the Dead Sea. This structure was identified by the archaeologists Yohanan Aharoni and Beno Rothenberg in 1957, and was dated by them to the Iron Age. In 2025, excavations were conducted at the site and the finds are attributed to the Seleucid period. The western structure is located on a cliff rising above the stream, and is called the "Roman" Metzad Zohar, but it is dated to the Crusader and Mamluk periods.
בקעת עוּבדה היא בקעה חולית מוקפת גבעות ב: The Ovda Valley is a sandy valley surrounded by hills in the southern Negev. The valley and the nearby Ovda Cliffs are named after Operation Uvda, which took place in 1949 toward the end of the War of Independence and in the course of which, among other things, its territory was captured. Together with the Sayarim Valley, the valley is one of the two valleys through which the main sections of Nahal Hiyyon pass. The valley is bounded on the south by the Sayarim Valley and on the north by the Timna Cliffs and the northern part of Mount Berech, on the east by Mount Shaharut, Mount Grofit and Mount Argaman, on the north by Mount Shahrur and Mount Perut, and on the west by the Ovda Cliffs.
שְׂדֵה נְחֶמְיָה הוא קיבוץ באצבע הגליל ב:
Sde Nehemia is a kibbutz in the Galilee Panhandle in the northern Hula Valley, about 5 km east of Kiryat Shmona, belonging to the Upper Galilee Regional Council.
The kibbutz was founded in 1940 by immigrants from Austria, Czechoslovakia and the Netherlands (who belonged to the Maccabi HaTza'ir youth movement), on land purchased from the Arab village of ad-Dawwara.
The kibbutz is named after Nehemia de Lieme, a Dutch Zionist activist who was chairman of the Dutch Zionist Federation in 1912–1918 and chairman of the KKL (Jewish National Fund) in 1919–1922.
תל חי הייתה חווה חקלאית קטנה באצבע הגליל: Tel Hai was a small agricultural farm in the Galilee Panhandle at the beginning of the period of Zionist settlement in the Land of Israel. On 1 March 1920 (11 Adar 5680), a battle took place there that became a symbol of the few fighting against the many and of the value of settlement as part of the Zionist ethos. Six Jews were killed in the battle, among them Joseph Trumpeldor. The farm, which became Kibbutz Tel Hai, was merged in 1926 with Kfar Giladi, and its members moved there. On the grounds of the courtyard, a memorial site, Tel-Hai Academic College, the Tel Hai Technological College, an industrial park and a youth hostel were established.
נַחַל יָגוּר הוא נחל אכזב הזורם במורדות: Nahal Yagur is an ephemeral stream flowing down the eastern slopes of Mount Carmel in the High Carmel and passing through "Ashdot Yagur Park", which is part of the Carmel Park. It is also called Wadi Shumariya after the fennel (shumar) bushes that grow in the area. The stream begins in the Isfiya area. It flows southeast of Nahal Ma'apilim toward the Zevulun Valley and empties into the Kishon River. On its way the stream passes through Kibbutz Yagur. Like the other Carmel streams flowing east of the mountain's watershed line, the stream is short, canyon-like and steep-banked. The stream is about 2 km long.
מאובן הוא שריד, תבנית או עקבות של בעל חי:
A fossil is the remains, impression or trace of an animal, plant or other organism from a past geological period that has been preserved in a petrified state. The field of science that studies fossils is paleontology.
The term fossil is usually reserved for remains older than 10,000 years, from before the end of the last ice age. (Later remains may be called subfossils.) Fossils provide important evidence for the precise dating of rock strata, and have supplied much of the information on which the current subdivisions of the geological time scale are based.
נַחַל תָּבוֹר (בערבית: ואדי אל־בִּירָה): Nahal Tavor (Arabic: Wadi al-Bira) is a perennial stream in the Lower Galilee, which originates in the area of Mount Ksulot in the Nazareth Hills, flows southeast and empties into the Jordan River near Tel Shoshan and near Kibbutz Gesher, about 3 km south of Naharayim. On its way it skirts Mount Tabor and drains many tributaries into itself, the main one being Nahal HaShiv'a. The stream forms a geographical boundary between the Sirin Plateau and the Kochav Plateau. In the lower section of the stream, included within the "Nahal Tavor" Nature Reserve, three springs emerge: Ein Rechesh, Ein Ze'ev and Ein Shahal.
נַחַל אֶשְׁתְּמֹעַ הוא נחל אכזב שראשיתו:
Nahal Eshtemoa is an ephemeral stream that begins in the southern Hebron Hills, at an elevation of about 800 meters above sea level, and ends at its confluence with Nahal Yatir, one of the tributaries of Nahal Be'er Sheva, near Hura.
The stream's name derives from the name of the biblical and Talmudic town of Eshtemoa, which is identified with the village of as-Samu, where the stream begins.
The stream's channel runs southwest; at its start it passes at the foot of the community of Shim'a, and further on at the foot of Mount Hiran and alongside the community of Meitar and the route of the Israel National Trail, and it includes several water pools (gevim); in addition, the Israel National Trail passes through the stream.
רכס רמים (מכונה גם בשם \"רכס מנרה\") הוא: The Ramim Ridge (also called the "Manara Ridge") is the central ridge of the Naftali Mountains in the Upper Galilee. The ridge, which runs north–south, lies within the territories of both Lebanon and Israel, and the border line between them passes through it. The ridge's eastern slope descends steeply toward the Hula Valley with an elevation difference of 750 meters over only about two kilometers, while the western slope descends gently toward Nahal Duba in Lebanese territory. Mount Shenan, rising to a height of 902 meters above sea level, is the ridge's summit. The Ramim Ridge is located north of the plateau area known as Ramot Naftali.
שְׁמוּרַת חַי-בָּר כַּרְמֶל הוא מוסד זוא:
The Hai-Bar Carmel Nature Reserve is a zoological institution of the hai-bar (wildlife reserve) type founded by the Nature Reserves Authority with the aim of protecting, and reintroducing to the wild, animals that once lived in northern Israel. Hai-Bar Carmel is located in the Carmel mountains in northern Israel, and it is the Mediterranean-climate counterpart of Hai-Bar Yotvata in the Arava.
In 1973 fencing began of a reserve area for Hai-Bar Carmel in the Nahal Galim basin. The Hai-Bar Carmel Reserve extends over an area of about 6,000 dunams. From Hai-Bar Carmel, the Persian fallow deer and the roe deer, which had disappeared from the country's landscape, have been released into the wild.
The institution's director is the zoologist Ben Rosenberg.
מכתש רמון הוא מכתש הסחיפה הגדול בעולם. ה:
Makhtesh Ramon is the largest erosion crater (makhtesh) in the world. It is located in Israel and is one of the five makhteshim of the Negev, and an International Dark Sky Reserve. The landscape of Makhtesh Ramon is unique. On the northern rim of the makhtesh lies the town of Mitzpe Ramon.
The makhtesh is about 40 km long, up to about 9 km wide and up to about 350 meters deep. In the east, the makhtesh is divided by Mount Ardon into two valleys: the Ardon Valley and the Mahmal Valley. Most of the makhtesh's area is drained by Nahal Ramon, which is called in Arabic "Wadi ar-Ruman", possibly because Romans passed through this area, on the Incense Route.
חולות כסוי הוא שטח המכוסה בחולות נודדים:
The Kasuy Sands (Holot Kasuy) are an area covered by shifting sand dunes located in the eastern Ovda Valley in the southern Negev, about a kilometer northeast of the Ovda base, about 5 km southwest of Mount Ayit and about 6 km north of the community of Shaharut. Together with the Samar Sands in the Arava, these are the only dunes in the Negev between Makhtesh Ramon and the Negev Highlands and Eilat.
The Israel National Trail passes through the dune area, where Mount Perut rises; north of the dunes runs Nahal Kasuy and to the south Nahal Yitro. The Kasuy Sands were formed by the drift of soft, light sand carried by strong winds and accumulated on these dunes, as in the Samar Sands.
דבורייה (בערבית: دبورية / دبوریه) היא מו:
Daburiyya (Arabic: دبورية / دبوریه) is a local council in the Northern District of Israel, located on the edge of the Jezreel Valley at the foot of Mount Tabor. The village of Daburiyya was declared a local council in 1961. According to the Central Bureau of Statistics, as of the end of 2022, all the residents of Daburiyya were Muslim Arabs.
Daburiyya is built on the slope of Mount Tabor, at its junction with the adjacent plain of the Ksulot Valley. Its form of construction is mainly rural, but it also has residential buildings and structures of one to four stories. The current head of the Daburiyya council is Rif'at Azaiza.
הַר תָּבוֹר הוא הר בגליל התחתון, מדרום ל:
Mount Tabor is a mountain in the Lower Galilee, south of the Nazareth Hills ridge and north of the Jezreel Valley. Its summit is 562 meters above sea level, and about 400 meters above its surroundings. The summit is prominent and visible from afar throughout the Galilee and even from the Golan Heights. Viewed from Kfar Tavor, from east to west, the summit appears pointed. Viewed from south to north, from the direction of Afula, the summit appears rounded and gentle.
On the mountain's slopes lie three communities: Umm al-Ghanam (at the southeastern end), Daburiyya (at the bottom of the western slope) and Shibli (at the bottom of the eastern slope), and east of it the moshava of Kfar Tavor.
יקבי כרמל (לשעבר \"כרמל מזרחי\", וקודם ל: Carmel Winery (formerly "Carmel Mizrahi", and before that "Carmel") is an Israeli wine-producing company that operates several wineries in Israel. Its first two wineries were established in 1889 in the moshavot of Rishon LeZion and Zichron Ya'akov by Baron Benjamin Edmond de Rothschild, and they are still active today. The company's logo depicts the spies sent by Moses to scout the land, who returned with a cluster of grapes "and they bore it between two upon a staff" (Numbers 13:23). The logo was originally purchased from the Efrat Winery, and the image was later also adopted by the Ministry of Tourism as the official symbol of Israeli tourism.
נחל צָפִית (בערבית: ואדי אלמֻראקאבּ) הוא:
Nahal Tzafit (Arabic: Wadi al-Muraqqab) is a stream channel in the northern Hatzera ridge near Metzad Tamar and Ma'ale Tamar, south of the Dead Sea. It is about 25 kilometers long. The stream's channel begins west of Mount Hatzera, descending at first northward and then eastward to the northern Arava. In its upper part the Ein Tzafit spring emerges. The stream descends over a high waterfall and several lower waterfalls to its lower section, as far as its outlet into Nahal Zin.
Until 1956 the stream was known by its Arabic name. That year the Government Names Committee set the name "Nahal Tzafit".
In April 1975 the stream was polluted by effluent that flowed from the Dead Sea Periclase plant.
סטף (בערבית: صطاف, בתעתיק לעברית: צטאף):
Sataf (Arabic: صطاف, transliterated into Hebrew as Tzataf) was an Arab village in the Jerusalem Hills on the eastern slope of Mount Eitan descending to Nahal Sorek, about ten kilometers west of Jerusalem. During the War of Independence the village was captured as part of Operation Dani, and its inhabitants left and were not permitted to return after the war.
The site lies about a kilometer northwest of Moshav Even Sapir, and preserves and reconstructs traditional and ancient hill agriculture that still exists in villages such as Battir and Wadi Fukin in the Judean Hills. Irrigated agriculture at the site was sustained mainly by the waters of two perched springs, Ein Sataf (Ein al-Balad) and Ein Bikura (Ein ash-Sharqiya).
עמק ססגון שוכן בצפון מזרח בקעת תמנע, כ-2: The Sasgon Valley lies in the northeastern Timna Valley, about 25 km north of Eilat and about 3 km west of Route 90, and west of Kibbutz Elifaz. Around the valley stand residual hills of Nubian sandstone, and the Israel National Trail passes through its heart. The valley lies outside the boundaries of Timna Park and is open to the public free of charge. From 2007 and for about a dozen years, a public struggle was waged against the construction of a hotel complex inside the valley. The struggle was crowned with success, and in December 2019 the National Planning and Building Council unanimously approved a plan under which the Sasgon Valley will be declared a nature reserve. Under this plan, the construction of a hotel will be permitted near the entrance to Timna Park.
